title: XXII-XXIV: theoretical and practical uses — Cap. 15 COMPLETE
pass_a_gloss: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): 2 Corinthians 10:18. 1 Corinthians 4:5; by means belonging toward ye argument belonging toward Psalm 7; — that ye conscience belonging toward things well done may be consoled against unjust judgments. that we may beware evils belonging toward fault; pedagogical, corrective, consolatory — that same we may live holily in God's eyes (Psalm 139); The other use stands as practical: XXIV. Augustine speaks belonging toward active science joined with will plus power. but because they stand as future they stand as known by means belonging toward God — Origen, Chrysostom, Ambrose; — things stand as not future because God knows them. who set absolute foreknowledge belonging toward things certainly future before ye divine decree, make it ye cause belonging toward things, plus out from ye certainty belonging toward divine foreknowledge take away ye contingency belonging toward things — and it refutes those who confuse ye distinct modes belonging toward divine science. For this doctrine confirms ye catholic faith concerning God's omniscience; XXIII. both toward confirmation belonging toward orthodox faith plus toward elenchus plus refutation belonging toward various error — the first stands as theoretical. there follows a manifold use. Still concerning mode: XXII.
pass_b_english: XXII. Still concerning mode: there follows a manifold use. The first is theoretical, both for confirmation of orthodox faith and for elenchus and refutation of various error. XXIII. For this doctrine confirms the catholic faith concerning God's omniscience; and it refutes those who confuse the distinct modes of divine science, who set absolute foreknowledge of things certainly future before the divine decree, make it the cause of things, and from the certainty of divine foreknowledge take away the contingency of things.

Things are not future because God knows them, but because they are future they are known by God — Origen, Chrysostom, Ambrose; Augustine speaks of active science joined with will and power. XXIV. The other use is practical: pedagogical, corrective, consolatory — that we may live holily in God's eyes (Psalm 139); that we may beware evils of fault; that the conscience of things well done may be consoled against unjust judgments, by the argument of Psalm 7; 1 Corinthians 4:5; 2 Corinthians 10:18.
source_text: XXII. Adhuc de modo: sequitur usus plurifarius. Primus est theoreticus, tum ad confirmationem fidei orthodoxae, tum ad elenchum et refutationem erroris varii. XXIII. Confirmat enim haec doctrina fidem catholicam de Dei omniscientia; et refutat eos qui distinctos divinae scientiae modos confundunt, praescientiam absolutam de rebus certo futuris decreto divino anteponunt, rerumque causam faciunt, et e certitudine divinae praescientiae rerum contingentiam tollunt. Res non ideo futurae quia Deus novit, sed quia futurae sunt a Deo cognoscuntur — Origenes, Chrysostomus, Ambrosius; Augustinus de scientia activa cum voluntate et potentia conjuncta loquitur. XXIV. Alter usus est practicus: paedeuticus, epanorthoticus, paracleticus — ut in oculis Dei sancte vivamus, Psal. CXXXIX; ut mala culpae caveamus; ut conscientia rerum bene gestarum adversus iniqua judicia consoletur, argumento Psal. VII; I Cor. IV.5; II Cor. X.18.
